questions.prompt: Why must the original message be obtained rather than a forwarded copy?
options: A forward loses the original headers, which carry the authentication results and routing path
questions.explanation: Headers are the primary analytic source for a phishing message, and forwarding replaces them with the forwarder's own -- so the original must be obtained as an attachment or pulled directly.

questions.prompt: What are the four distinct populations this playbook warns against conflating?
options: Received, opened, clicked, and submitted credentials
Windows, macOS, mobile, and web users
questions.explanation: Each is smaller and more severe than the last. Conflating them either overstates the incident or misses actual victims who need credential resets.

questions.prompt: When does a single reported phishing email become an organization-wide incident?
options: Whenever more than one person receives it
When anyone submitted credentials, anyone executed a payload, or the message bypassed controls that should have caught it
Never; phishing is always a helpdesk ticket
questions.explanation: Any of these three conditions means the impact extends beyond the reporting user -- including the third, since a control gap means the next message will also get through.

questions.prompt: Why should every user who clicked be treated as a possible credential submitter unless proven otherwise?
options: Only the phishing infrastructure knows who actually submitted, so submission cannot be confirmed from your own telemetry
Submitters and clickers are always the same population
questions.explanation: Click telemetry from mail security or proxy logs identifies clickers, but what happened on the attacker's page is not visible to you -- so the safe assumption runs one tier up.
